name: Malola Narasimha Temple, Ahobilam
deity: Vishnu as Malola Narasimha — seated with Lakshmi on his lap, the Lord 'beloved of Lakshmi'
period: One of the Nava Narasimha shrines of Ahobilam in the Nallamala hills of Andhra Pradesh
summary: On the Vedadri hill above Upper Ahobilam, Malola Narasimha is the gentle face of the lion-lord — seated with Lakshmi on his lap, the beloved of Ma whose festival image travels with the jeeyars of the Ahobila Matha.

sections.history: Malola Narasimha is one of the Nava Narasimha of Ahobilam, set on the Vedadri, or Vedachala, hill about two kilometres from the Upper Ahobilam temple; the shrine is also known as Markanda Lakshmi Kshetra. Its fame reaches far beyond the hill. Tradition in the Ahobila Matha holds that its founder, Adivan Satakopa Jeeyar, who lived in the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, received the festival image of Malola Narasimha here as the deity he was to carry. Ever since, the utsava murti of Malola has accompanied the matha's pontiffs, the Azhagiya Singars, on their journeys across India — so this small hill shrine is the home of a Lord who travels.
sections.architecture: The temple is a small stone shrine on a shelf of the hill, approached by a rough path and steps. In the sanctum Narasimha is seated with his left leg folded and his right leg hanging down, and Lakshmi sits upon the folded knee, held close in the Lord's embrace. The calm of the image is the meaning of the place: here the fierce form has grown serene in the presence of his consort.
sections.legends: The name explains the shrine: Ma is Lakshmi and lola means beloved, so Malola is the one dear to Lakshmi. Tradition holds that after the fury of the battle with Hiranyakashipu, Lakshmi came to the Lord here and his anger was stilled in her company. The story of the festival image coming into the hands of Adivan Satakopa Jeeyar is told with great affection within the Ahobila Matha. In the astrological reading of the nine shrines, Malola is linked with Venus.
sections.festivals: Narasimha Jayanti and the annual Brahmotsavam of Ahobilam are observed at all the hill shrines. The travelling festival image of Malola is worshipped wherever the Ahobila Matha's pontiff is in residence, so many of its celebrations take place far from the hill itself. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: The climb from Upper Ahobilam is shorter than the trail to Jwala but still steep and stony in places. The shrine is quiet and intimate, and the view back over the forested valley rewards the effort. Wear comfortable footwear, carry water, and combine the visit with the other Upper Ahobilam shrines.

visit.timings: Worship is offered daily; the shrine is reached on foot and is best visited in daylight. Confirm current timings locally.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: From Lower Ahobilam (reached by road via Allagadda; Nandyal is the nearest major railhead), go up to Upper Ahobilam by local transport. Malola lies about two kilometres beyond the Upper Ahobilam temple, by a steep path on foot.
